lessons.title: தலை, கை — head and hand, both Tamil's own
lessons.gloss: head and hand — both native Dravidian words, unlike Hindi's Sanskrit-descended pair

segments.text: You've seen Hindi's sir and hāth trace all the way back to Sanskrit. Tamil's words for the same two body parts tell a simpler story: both are native.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The words

segments.text: தலை (talai) = "head" — native Dravidian.
கை (kai) = "hand" — native Dravidian.
Neither is borrowed from Sanskrit, unlike Hindi's sir (< Sanskrit śiras) or hāth (< Sanskrit hasta). Tamil simply kept its own words for two of the most basic parts of the body.

segments.instruction: the contrast — Hindi borrowed these from Sanskrit; Tamil didn't
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the contrast — Hindi borrowed these from Sanskrit; Tamil didn't]

segments.text: What are Tamil's words for head and hand? (தலை talai, கை kai.) Are either of these Sanskrit loans? (No — both native Dravidian, unlike Hindi's Sanskrit-descended sir and hāth.)

lessons.title: க (ka) — the letter that is three bowls
lessons.gloss: the single letter க — met, then written

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: க and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: say the sound of ற.
One letter this time. Just one.

The most-used consonant in Tamil, and the most built: a square frame on top, then two bowls hanging under it. Three pen-down runs. Take it slowly — nothing else in this book asks for as many separate pieces.
க — ka.
What it is made of:
an upper square frame.
a large lower-left bowl.
a lower-right bowl with an open foot.
வணக்கம் has it twice, doubled in the middle.
1. start at the middle left and climb the left upright.
2. without lifting, carry the top bar to the right and return along it to the inner corner.
3. without lifting, drop the inner upright and carry the middle bar left — then lift once.
4. set the pen at the inner crossing and curve down and around the lower-left bowl.
5. without lifting again, return up its outer left side — then lift a second time.
6. set the pen at the inner crossing and turn around the lower-right bowl — and only now lift.
Pen lifts: 2. The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

Stroke order is one attested teaching order, not a national standard — Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 3, க (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 191.

segments.instruction: க (ka) once, slowly, following the steps above
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: க once, slowly, following the steps above]

segments.instruction: it twice more, without looking back at the steps
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: it twice more, without looking back at the steps]

segments.text: How many pen lifts does க (ka) take? (Two — three separate runs.) What are the three parts? (Upper frame, lower-left bowl, lower-right bowl.)

lessons.title: ி and நன்றி — replace the vowel, then hear ndr
lessons.gloss: replace the inherent vowel with i, assemble நன்றி, and hear nasal-triggered voicing

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
waitUntilStopped: Script you'll notice: The first vowel sign
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: The first vowel sign, Script you'll notice: Assemble நன்றி and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: A consonant can keep a or lose it under a puḷḷi. The third option is to replace it with a vowel sign.

blocks.title: Script you'll notice: The first vowel sign

segments.text: ற = ṟa becomes றி = ṟi.

ி is a hook above and to the right. The consonant keeps its shape; the sign hangs from it. Later, ை (ai) will appear before its consonant on the page but after it in speech, the same eye/ear trap as Devanagari ि.
ந, ன், றி becomes நன்றி.

utterances: piece: ந, na — dental, last lesson.
piece: ன், ṉ — alveolar, with puḷḷi, Lessons 3–4.
piece: றி, ṟi — ற plus the i-sign, this lesson.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: Why nandri has a d-sound

segments.text: ன் + ற is pronounced close to ndr. This follows a broader Tamil rule: a nasal voices the stop after it.
Each n-letter creates its own cluster. That payoff explains both the three spellings and the common English romanization nandri, whose d is heard but not separately written.

segments.instruction: றி — ற plus the hook above right
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: றி — ற plus the hook above right]

segments.text: What are a consonant's three vowel choices? (Keep inherent a, remove it with puḷḷi, or replace it with a vowel sign.) Where does ி attach? (Above and right.) Why is naṉṟi often written nandri? (ன் + ற is pronounced ndr because a nasal voices the following stop.)

lessons.title: ர — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ர — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ர and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ச — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ர — ra.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not r, it is ra.
You already say these, and every one of them has ர (ra) somewhere inside it:
வணக்கம் / நமஸ்காரம் vaṇakkam / namaskāram — Tamil kept a native bow-word where its neighbors borrowed Sanskrit.
சரி sari — okay / alright / correct (sari).
ஆம் / இல்லை / சரி ām / illai / sari — answering in Tamil.
பெயர் peyar — name.

blocks.title: Writing: ர — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ர (ra) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
